VIDEO.title: What Everyone MISSED About “Render to Caesar”
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Matthew 22:15-46 · Episode 44 (#47 of 58 in the playlist)
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 22:15-46, four questions in the temple. The Pharisees' disciples and the Herodians ask whether it is lawful to pay the tax to Caesar; Jesus asks for a denarius and says, 'render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's; and to God the things that are God's.' The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, ask about a woman married to seven brothers; Jesus says they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God, and quotes Exodus 3:6. A scholar of the Law asks for the great commandment; Jesus answers with love for God and love for neighbor. Then Jesus asks them how David can call his own son 'Lord' in Psalm 110:1, and no one dares ask Him anything more.

The tax question is a trap. Say 'pay' and lose the crowd, who hated Roman rule and Deuteronomy 17:15 forbade a foreign king; say 'don't pay' and the Herodians report Him to Rome. The coin of Tiberius carried his image and called him son of the divine Augustus, and on the other side 'chief priest.'

The Sadducees accepted only the Torah as binding, so Jesus answers from the Torah: God is still the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so they are alive to Him. In the resurrection people are like the angels, which the Sadducees also denied (Acts 23:8).
The great commandment joins the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:5) with Leviticus 19:18. Psalm 110 shows David's son is also David's Lord, and a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
The lesson: whenever people in authority claim what belongs to God, God must always take priority. Like Daniel and his friends, honor the king, but worship God alone.
QUOTES: Whenever people in authority claim what belongs to God, God must always take priority.
Tiberius is considered by the Romans to be the son of a god. And here is Jesus, the son of the true God.
Why does Jesus ask to see that coin? Why that coin and why inside the temple?
If we're not careful here, friends, we can let that become the authority that we give tribute to.

method.h: Answer from the source they trust
method.p: Jesus answers each group on its own ground: the coin they carry, the Torah the Sadducees accept, and the psalm the Pharisees read as messianic.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Therefore, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s; and to God the things that are God’s.
He is not the God of the dead but of the living.
We must obey God rather than men.

src.text: And they *sent their disciples to Him, along with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that You are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and defer to no one; for You are not partial to any. Therefore, tell us, what do You think? Is it lawful to give a tax to Caesar, or not?”

lines.text: Pharisees and Herodians were natural enemies, joined to trap Him. A 'yes' turns the crowd against Him; a 'no' is sedition the Herodians can report.
Many Jews held that a foreign king was forbidden: 'you may not put a foreigner over yourselves who is not your brother' (Deuteronomy 17:15).
Matthew's word is kēnsos, the Roman census or poll tax; Luke 20:22 uses phoros, 'taxes' or tribute.

src.text: Show Me the coin used for the tax.” And they brought Him a denarius. And He *said to them, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” They *said to Him, “Caesar’s.” Then He *said to them, “Therefore, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s; and to God the things that are God’s.”

lines.text: Jesus doesn't carry one; they do. The coin of Tiberius bore his head and the words 'Tiberius Caesar Augustus, son of the divine Augustus.' On the reverse sat a woman, often read as Livia as Pax, with PONTIF MAXIM: chief priest.
The contrast is deliberate: Tiberius claimed to be the son of a god, and here stands Jesus, the Son of the true God.
Many readers add: the coin bears Caesar's image, but people bear the image of God (Genesis 1:27), so they belong to God.

left.text: Render to all what is due them: tax to whom tax is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honor to whom honor.

right.text: But Peter and the apostles answered and said, “We must obey God rather than men.

lines.text: God sets up rulers: 'By me kings reign' (Proverbs 8:15); 'He removes kings and establishes kings' (Daniel 2:21).

But when a ruler claims what is God's, God comes first. Daniel's friends served Babylon but would not bow: 'we are not going to serve your gods' (Daniel 3:18). Esther too risked her life before the king.
1 Peter 2:17 holds both together: 'fear God, honor the king.'

left.text: saying, “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies having no children, his brother as next of kin shall marry his wife and raise up a seed for his brother.’

right.text: “If brothers live together and one of them dies and has no son, then the wife of the one who died shall not be married outside the family to a strange man. Her husband’s brother shall go in to her and take her to himself as wife and perform the duty of a husband’s brother to her.

lines.text: The Sadducees, priestly aristocrats who accepted only the Torah as binding, use the law of the husband's brother to make resurrection look absurd.
The Mishnah later lists among those with no share in the world to come: 'One who says: There is no resurrection of the dead derived from the Torah' (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1).

left.text: For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.

right.text: For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor an angel, nor a spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all.

lines.text: You are mistaken, Jesus says, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God. And He answers with angels, which they also denied.
Daniel 12:2 already promised that 'many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground will awake.' Daniel sits among the Writings in the Hebrew Bible.

left.text: He said also, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Then Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.

right.text: ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead but of the living.”

lines.text: Jesus argues from the Torah, the books they accept. 'I am,' not 'I was': the patriarchs live to God.
The Talmud tells of Rabban Gamliel proving resurrection to heretics 'from the Torah, from the Prophets, and from Writings' (Talmud Sanhedrin 90b).

left.text: And He said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.’

right.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.

lines.text: Jesus quotes the Shema, said daily by faithful Jews. Matthew has 'mind' where Deuteronomy has 'might'; Mark 12:30 includes both mind and strength.
The second is like it: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' (Leviticus 19:18), which Leviticus 19:34 extends to the sojourner.
Hillel's famous summary is the negative form: 'That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation' (Talmud Shabbat 31a).

left.text: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, / “Sit at My right hand, / Until I put Your enemies beneath Your feet”’?

right.text: Yahweh says to my Lord: / “Sit at My right hand / Until I put Your enemies as a footstool for Your feet.”

lines.text: If the Messiah is only David's son, why does David call him 'my Lord'? Chrysostom said Jesus 'thus introduces David proclaiming His Godhead.'
Psalm 110 goes on: 'You are a priest forever / According to the order of Melchizedek' (110:4). The true King is also the true Priest, the very title Caesar's coin claimed.

src.text: And no one was able to answer Him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day on to ask Him another question.

lines.text: The hidden struggle may not be the government but giving people the authority to approve our words and actions: the likes, the subscribes, the accolades, the applause.
Whenever people in authority claim what belongs to God, God must always take priority.

TERMS.def: Jews who backed Herod's family, and with it Roman rule.
Roman silver coin, about a day's wage, stamped with the emperor's image.
'Chief priest,' a title the emperors held and put on their coins.
Priestly party that denied resurrection and angels.
A brother marrying his dead brother's childless widow (Deuteronomy 25:5-10).
'Hear, O Israel' (Deuteronomy 6:4-9), the daily confession of faith.
King of Salem and priest of God Most High (Genesis 14:18); Psalm 110:4.

To love. Look up: BDAG, ἀγαπάω.

BACKGROUND.p: The common silver denarius of Tiberius shows his laureate head with 'TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS' (Tiberius Caesar Augustus, son of the divine Augustus), and on the reverse a seated woman with 'PONTIF MAXIM' (chief priest). For many Jews the image and the claims were offensive.
The Mishnah names Tyrian coinage as the standard for sanctuary payments (Mishnah Bekhorot 8:7), which is one reason money changers worked in the temple courts.
Josephus describes Herod the Great building temples to Augustus at Caesarea Maritima, at Sebaste in Samaria, and at Paneas near the springs of the Jordan. He did not build one in Jerusalem.

DEBATES.p: Some read 22:21 as dividing life into civil and religious spheres. Others, like the video, read it as putting Caesar's claim inside God's: the coin may be Caesar's, but Caesar, like every person, belongs to God.

DEBATES.h: Who is the woman on the coin?
DEBATES.p: The seated figure on the reverse is often identified as Livia, Tiberius's mother, portrayed as Pax; numismatists debate it.
Some see the argument as resting on the present tense ('I am'); others on God's covenant faithfulness, which death cannot end.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The idea that simply owning the tribute coin proved emperor worship is offered without a source.
Herod built temples to Augustus at Caesarea, Sebaste and Paneas, not 'around Jerusalem.'
The claim that Roman coins were forbidden in the temple is given without a source; the Mishnah names Tyrian coinage as the standard for sanctuary payments (Bekhorot 8:7).
The video says Hillel and Shammai argued over the greatest commandment; no source is given. The best-known related saying is Hillel's summary in Talmud Shabbat 31a.
Daniel is counted among the Prophets in English Bibles but among the Writings in the Hebrew Bible.
The video's translation reads 'tribute' in Luke 20:22; the LSB has 'taxes.'

QUESTIONS: Why was the tax question such a clever trap?
What belongs to Caesar, and what belongs to God, in your life?
Why did Jesus answer the Sadducees from Exodus rather than from Daniel?
How does loving God with all your mind change how you study?
Who is the 'sojourner' you are called to love as yourself (Leviticus 19:34)?
Where are you tempted to pay tribute to people or platforms that claim what belongs to God?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson: whenever people in authority claim what belongs to God, God must always take priority. God puts pagans in positions of authority, so His people may concede to some of their demands, but not when they claim what is God's. Daniel and his friends, and Esther, faced the same choice, and the apostles said, 'We must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29). For many the hidden struggle is the likes, the accolades and the applause of others; if we're not careful, that becomes the authority we give tribute to.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): look at where your time and attention went yesterday. Give God the first portion today, and pray by name for one person in authority over you (1 Timothy 2:1-2).

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 22:15-46, four questions in the temple. The Pharisees' disciples and the Herodians ask whether it is lawful to pay the tax to Caesar; Jesus asks for a denarius and says, 'render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's; and to God the things that are God's.' The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, ask about a woman married to seven brothers; Jesus says they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God, and quotes Exodus 3:6. A scholar of the Law asks for the great commandment; Jesus answers with love for God and love for neighbor. Then Jesus asks them how David can call his own son 'Lord' in Psalm 110:1, and no one dares ask Him anything more.
- The tax question is a trap. Say 'pay' and lose the crowd, who hated Roman rule and Deuteronomy 17:15 forbade a foreign king; say 'don't pay' and the Herodians report Him to Rome. The coin of Tiberius carried his image and called him son of the divine Augustus, and on the other side 'chief priest.'
- The Sadducees accepted only the Torah as binding, so Jesus answers from the Torah: God is still the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so they are alive to Him. In the resurrection people are like the angels, which the Sadducees also denied (Acts 23:8).
- The great commandment joins the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:5) with Leviticus 19:18. Psalm 110 shows David's son is also David's Lord, and a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
- The lesson: whenever people in authority claim what belongs to God, God must always take priority. Like Daniel and his friends, honor the king, but worship God alone.

   (video) Jesus argues from the Torah, the books they accept. 'I am,' not 'I was': the patriarchs live to God.

## The great commandment and David's Lord
1. Matthew 22:34-40; Deuteronomy 6:5: The great commandment
   Jesus (Matthew 22:37, LSB): "And He said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.’"
   Moses (Deuteronomy 6:5, LSB): "You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might."
   (video) Jesus quotes the Shema, said daily by faithful Jews. Matthew has 'mind' where Deuteronomy has 'might'; Mark 12:30 includes both mind and strength. (Mark 12:30)
   (video) The second is like it: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' (Leviticus 19:18), which Leviticus 19:34 extends to the sojourner. (Leviticus 19:18; Leviticus 19:34)
   [Background] Hillel's famous summary is the negative form: 'That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation' (Talmud Shabbat 31a).
2. Matthew 22:41-45; Psalm 110:1: David's son, David's Lord
   Jesus (Matthew 22:44, LSB): "‘The Lord said to my Lord, / “Sit at My right hand, / Until I put Your enemies beneath Your feet”’?"
   David (Psalm 110:1, LSB): "Yahweh says to my Lord: / “Sit at My right hand / Until I put Your enemies as a footstool for Your feet.”"
   (video) If the Messiah is only David's son, why does David call him 'my Lord'? Chrysostom said Jesus 'thus introduces David proclaiming His Godhead.'
   (video) Psalm 110 goes on: 'You are a priest forever / According to the order of Melchizedek' (110:4). The true King is also the true Priest, the very title Caesar's coin claimed. (Psalm 110:4)
3. Matthew 22:21, 46: What tribute are you paying?
   Lesson Matthew 22:46: "And no one was able to answer Him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day on to ask Him another question." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+22:46
   (video) The hidden struggle may not be the government but giving people the authority to approve our words and actions: the likes, the subscribes, the accolades, the applause.
   (video) Whenever people in authority claim what belongs to God, God must always take priority.

## Key people
- The Pharisees' disciples: Sent with the Herodians to trap Him. [Background] Pharisees resented Roman rule but tolerated it.
- The Herodians: Supporters of Herod's dynasty, and so of Rome. [Background] They also plot with Pharisees in Mark 3:6.
- Caesar (Tiberius): The emperor whose face and titles were on the denarius. [Background] Tiberius reigned AD 14-37.
- The Sadducees: Deny resurrection and angels; accept only the Torah as binding. [Background] Many of the chief priests were Sadducees (Acts 5:17).
- The scholar of the Law: Asks which is the great commandment. [Background] In Mark 12:34 Jesus tells him he is not far from the kingdom.
- David: Calls the Messiah 'my Lord' in Psalm 110:1. [Background] Jesus says David spoke 'in the Spirit' (22:43).

## Places [Background]
- Jerusalem (named in the video): The temple courts, where the four questions are asked.
- Caesarea Maritima: Herod's port city, with a temple to Rome and Augustus; seat of the Roman governor.
- Sebaste (Samaria): Rebuilt by Herod and named for Augustus (Greek Sebastos), with a temple to him.
- Caesarea Philippi (Paneas): Herod built a temple to Augustus here.

## Key terms
- Herodians: Jews who backed Herod's family, and with it Roman rule.
- Denarius: Roman silver coin, about a day's wage, stamped with the emperor's image.
- Pontifex maximus: 'Chief priest,' a title the emperors held and put on their coins.
- Sadducees: Priestly party that denied resurrection and angels.
- Levirate marriage: A brother marrying his dead brother's childless widow (Deuteronomy 25:5-10).
- Shema: 'Hear, O Israel' (Deuteronomy 6:4-9), the daily confession of faith.
- Melchizedek: King of Salem and priest of God Most High (Genesis 14:18); Psalm 110:4.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- The tribute coin: The common silver denarius of Tiberius shows his laureate head with 'TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS' (Tiberius Caesar Augustus, son of the divine Augustus), and on the reverse a seated woman with 'PONTIF MAXIM' (chief priest). For many Jews the image and the claims were offensive.
- Coins in the temple: The Mishnah names Tyrian coinage as the standard for sanctuary payments (Mishnah Bekhorot 8:7), which is one reason money changers worked in the temple courts.
- Herod's temples to Augustus: Josephus describes Herod the Great building temples to Augustus at Caesarea Maritima, at Sebaste in Samaria, and at Paneas near the springs of the Jordan. He did not build one in Jerusalem.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "For this is not to give but to render, and this He shows both by the image, and by the superscription." Homilies on Matthew 70, on 22:21. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "But not because they do not marry, therefore are they angels, but because they are as angels, therefore they do not marry." Homilies on Matthew 70, on 22:30. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "He thus introduces David proclaiming His Godhead." Homilies on Matthew 71, on 22:43-45. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Two kingdoms or one Lord? Some read 22:21 as dividing life into civil and religious spheres. Others, like the video, read it as putting Caesar's claim inside God's: the coin may be Caesar's, but Caesar, like every person, belongs to God.
- Who is the woman on the coin? The seated figure on the reverse is often identified as Livia, Tiberius's mother, portrayed as Pax; numismatists debate it.
- Why Exodus 3:6? Some see the argument as resting on the present tense ('I am'); others on God's covenant faithfulness, which death cannot end.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The idea that simply owning the tribute coin proved emperor worship is offered without a source.
- Herod built temples to Augustus at Caesarea, Sebaste and Paneas, not 'around Jerusalem.'
- The claim that Roman coins were forbidden in the temple is given without a source; the Mishnah names Tyrian coinage as the standard for sanctuary payments (Bekhorot 8:7).
- The video says Hillel and Shammai argued over the greatest commandment; no source is given. The best-known related saying is Hillel's summary in Talmud Shabbat 31a.
- Daniel is counted among the Prophets in English Bibles but among the Writings in the Hebrew Bible.
- The video's translation reads 'tribute' in Luke 20:22; the LSB has 'taxes.'

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why was the tax question such a clever trap?
2. What belongs to Caesar, and what belongs to God, in your life?
3. Why did Jesus answer the Sadducees from Exodus rather than from Daniel?
4. How does loving God with all your mind change how you study?
5. Who is the 'sojourner' you are called to love as yourself (Leviticus 19:34)?
6. Where are you tempted to pay tribute to people or platforms that claim what belongs to God?

## Application
- (video) The lesson: whenever people in authority claim what belongs to God, God must always take priority. God puts pagans in positions of authority, so His people may concede to some of their demands, but not when they claim what is God's. Daniel and his friends, and Esther, faced the same choice, and the apostles said, 'We must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29). For many the hidden struggle is the likes, the accolades and the applause of others; if we're not careful, that becomes the authority we give tribute to.
- Study note (added): look at where your time and attention went yesterday. Give God the first portion today, and pray by name for one person in authority over you (1 Timothy 2:1-2).
